# Decisions

The Phase 0 decision record. Each entry says what was decided, when, and what it
changes. Background for every item is in [`plan.md`](plan.md), which was written
before some of these decisions and assumes an EU company; where they differ,
this file wins.

## Settled

| # | Decision | Date | Consequence |
|---|---|---|---|
| D1 | **A Norwegian company shipping from Norway.** | 2026-09-23 | Norway is the home market. Sales to Sweden and Denmark are exports into the EU, with EU import VAT and customs on every parcel (see below). Replaces the earlier assumption of an EU company. |
| D2 | **Launch in Norway, Sweden and Denmark.** | 2026-09-23 | These three markets are active (NOK, SEK, DKK; nb-NO, sv-SE, da-DK). The other 25 exist but are inactive; Germany was dropped from the launch list and can be switched back on in one line. |
| D3 | **Payments: Stripe.** Checkout Sessions with the Payment Element, Stripe Tax for VAT. | 2026-09-23 | Keeps card data off our servers (PCI DSS SAQ A). Local methods are configured per market in Stripe. `products.tax_code` holds the Stripe Tax code. |
| D4 | **Commerce core built from scratch**, not on an open-source platform. | 2026-09-23 | We own catalogue, pricing, carts, orders, returns and promotions. |
| D5 | **Changes go straight to `main`**, which deploys to production. | 2026-09-23 | Fine while the site is a placeholder. Revisit before launch: switch to pull requests with preview deployments. |
| D6 | **Region: Ireland.** Supabase `eu-west-1`; Vercel functions pinned to `dub1`. | 2026-09-23 | Both in the EU/EEA; functions sit next to the database. |
| D7 | **One Next.js app**, not a monorepo. | 2026-09-23 | Split into packages when a second deployable (such as the MCP server in Phase 4) needs shared domain code. |
| D8 | **Commerce data in a private `commerce` schema**, reached only by server code over a direct connection. | 2026-09-23 | Supabase's Data API never exposes it; row-level security is on with no policies as a backstop. |
| D9 | **Drizzle schema is the source of truth**; migrations are generated into `supabase/migrations` and applied to Supabase by Claude as they land. | 2026-09-23 | CI fails if schema and migrations disagree. |
| D10 | **Data residency: EU/EEA vendors wherever a comparable option exists.** A US processor only with a DPA and the EU–US Data Privacy Framework or standard contractual clauses. | 2026-09-23 | Default set by Claude. Every vendor is listed in [`residency-register.md`](residency-register.md) before it touches production data. |
| D11 | **Build to WCAG 2.2 AA.** | 2026-09-23 | Meets Norway's universal-design rules and the European Accessibility Act for Swedish and Danish customers. |
| D12 | **Kaizen Store is a multi-purpose template**, not tied to one product category. | 2026-09-23 | VAT comes from a Stripe Tax code per product (with a per-variant override); every goods withdrawal exclusion is available; producer responsibility schemes are tracked per product with registrations per market; `commerce.missing_registrations` shows the gaps per store. Variants carry a customs tariff (HS) code and country of origin for export declarations. |
| D13 | **No extra monitoring or analytics accounts until there is a need.** | 2026-09-23 | Errors: Vercel's built-in logs. Speed: Vercel Speed Insights. Traffic: Vercel Web Analytics (cookieless). Business events: our own tables in Postgres. Experiments: assignment in our own code. Sentry, PostHog and GrowthBook are optional add-ons, not prerequisites. |
| D14 | **No non-essential cookies at launch.** | 2026-09-23 | Cart and session cookies are strictly necessary and need no consent, so the store needs no cookie banner. Adding marketing pixels or cookie-based analytics later brings back the consent requirement. Default set by Claude. |
| D15 | **Payment settings belong to the store owner, in the store's admin.** API keys and webhook secrets per payment provider, test or live mode, and an on/off switch per payment method (per market) are edited in store settings, not in Vercel environment variables. | 2026-09-24 | Needs an admin area with sign-in (Phase 1c). Secrets are stored encrypted in the database with a key held only in the server environment, never returned to the browser once saved, and every change is logged. The only payment-related environment variable is that encryption key. |
| D16 | **Checkout on Stripe's hosted page, with each store's own Stripe account.** Kaizen places the order and holds the stock, then hands over to Stripe Checkout; a webhook (created automatically in the owner's Stripe account when they save their secret key) confirms payment. | 2026-09-24 | Card data never touches Kaizen (PCI DSS SAQ A). Orders are numbered per store from 1001. Stock is held for 35 minutes (the session's 30 plus a margin). VAT shown on orders uses each country's standard rate until Stripe Tax is connected; reduced rates are not applied yet (see R6). |
| D17 | **Stripe Connect: each store sells through its own connected Stripe account, created by Kaizen.** Replaces the pasted keys of D15 and D16. Configured as Stripe advises for Shopify-like platforms: Accounts v2, full Stripe Dashboard for the store, Stripe collects its fees from the store and carries negative balances, direct charges (the store is the seller), onboarding with Stripe's embedded components in the admin. | 2026-09-24 | Stores no longer paste Stripe keys, and Kaizen stores no store secrets: only Kaizen's own platform keys (`STRIPE_SECRET_KEY_TEST`/`_LIVE`, `STRIPE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY_TEST`/`_LIVE`) in Vercel. Two platform webhooks per mode, created from the platform page: payment events from stores' accounts, and Accounts v2 events that keep each store's status (`stripe_accounts`) current. Kaizen takes a platform-wide fee per sale as an application fee (`platform_settings.sale_fee_bps`, 0 until set); monthly plans come next with Stripe Billing. Payment methods are chosen in each store's Stripe Dashboard (dynamic payment methods), so the per-market switches of D15 are gone. Optional invoice PDF per order (Stripe Invoicing). VAT stays Kaizen's own calculation for now; Stripe Tax per store waits for tax advice on Norway-to-EU sales. Old per-store keys and webhooks stay in the database only so payments started before the switch still complete. |
| D18 | **Kaizen's plans for stores are managed in Kaizen and billed with Stripe Billing.** Platform admins create plans (tiers) with monthly and yearly prices per currency, excluding VAT, and a fee per sale; saving copies them to Stripe as Products and Prices. Admins start, change and cancel each store's plan and can give a store its own fee. | 2026-09-24 | The subscription lives on Kaizen's Stripe account with the store's own connected account as the customer (`customer_account`); Stripe emails an invoice each period, due in 14 days (`send_invoice`), with 25 % Norwegian VAT for stores in Norway and none for others (reverse charge); since 5 November 2026 nothing is billed to a store without its country (`NO_COUNTRY`: a plan, a premium theme or a domain waits, and Billing says where to add it), never taken to be Norway, and the business details ask for the country with none chosen. Store owners see their plan under Plan and open Stripe's customer portal for invoices and card details. A third platform webhook keeps `store_billing` current. The fee on a sale is the store's own fee, else its plan's while it is on the plan, else the platform default. Prices never change in place: a new amount is a new Stripe Price, and stores keep the old one until moved. Taking fees straight from a store's Stripe balance is left for when Stripe offers it outside preview. |
| D19 | **Owners choose their own plan, and can own several stores.** On a store's Plan page the owner picks a plan (monthly or yearly, in the store's currency) and pays by card through Stripe Checkout; later changes apply at once with proration, and they can cancel at the end of the period. An owner can create more stores from All stores, each a copy of the demo with its own Stripe account and plan. | 2026-09-24 | Plans still belong to a store, not a person. Platform admins can still put a store on an invoiced plan (D18). Only people who already own a store, or run the platform, can create stores (up to 10 each), so the beta stays invite-only (P3). `stores` is a reserved store address. |
| D20 | **Test payments need nothing from the store owner.** Kaizen sets up each store's test Stripe account itself, filled with Stripe's test values (date of birth 1901-01-01, address `address_full_match`, website `https://accessible.stripe.com`, test IBAN `NO9386011117947`) and Kaizen's acceptance of the service agreement, so test purchases land in the store's own test account straight away. Stripe's real identity checks happen only for the live account, before real money. New stores start with test payments on. | 2026-09-24 | Test accounts differ from live ones: no Stripe Dashboard, and Kaizen holds the fee and loss settings (Stripe allows this in test only because nothing real is at stake); live accounts stay as in D17. The account is created in the background when an owner opens the admin or Payments (the service agreement needs the owner's IP address); Stripe checks the test values within a minute or two, and a checkout in that window asks Stripe again rather than failing on an old status. Kaizen marks the accounts it made (`managed_by_kaizen`) and keeps Stripe's latest reasons (`requirements`, no personal data) so a stuck account can be explained. An older test account that waited for the owner's details is replaced; plans keep billing the account their subscription was started on. The storefront says when it is in test mode. |
| D21 | **Search and sharing are built in, for Kaizen and every store.** Every page has its title, description, canonical and hreflang links, Open Graph and X tags, and schema.org data: the store as an `OnlineStore` with its return policy, each market home as a `WebSite` and product list, each product as a `Product` (or a `ProductGroup` when variants differ by colour, size, material or pattern) with price, stock, shipping to the market, return policy and breadcrumbs. The site serves `robots.txt`, a sitemap index with one sitemap per open store (hreflang and pictures included), and `llms.txt` for Kaizen and for each store (terms, markets, shipping and every product with its price). Owners set their front page's title and description per language, a share picture, social profiles, AI crawler choices, extra crawler rules, their own llms.txt text and search console codes under Search; products get their own search title and description per language. Kaizen's own pages are set under Platform → Search. | 2026-09-24 | Everything is filled in from the store's data when the owner writes nothing; a page without a picture shares one Kaizen draws. Until stores have their own addresses (P2), crawlers read only the site's robots.txt, so each store's rules are added to it under the store's path, and the rules for everyone are repeated in each crawler's group (a crawler follows only its own group). AI assistants and AI search are welcome by default and can be turned off separately from AI training. Carts, order pages and the admin are left out; stores not yet opened, or hidden by their owner, are `noindex` and left out of sitemaps and llms.txt. The 14-day return policy states the legal right of withdrawal, with return costs on the shopper (the legal default) until stores can set their own terms (Phase 1d). A blog or other content types will use the same fields when they are built. |
| D22 | **Shoppers pay on Kaizen's own checkout page, with Stripe's payment form.** The cart's checkout button places the order as before and opens a Stripe Checkout Session with `ui_mode: "elements"` on the store's own Stripe account; the shopper then pays at `/{market}/checkout` on the store's site: Kaizen's order summary, then Stripe's express buttons (Apple Pay, Google Pay, Link, Klarna where offered), contact, delivery address and payment Elements, in the store's colours and the market's language. Paying leads to the order page as before. Stripe's hosted page stays as a platform-wide fallback (Platform → Stripe). | 2026-09-24 | Stripe's recommended way to build a custom checkout: the session still carries prices, shipping, Kaizen's fee, the invoice and the payment methods each store has turned on, and orders are still confirmed by Stripe's events, so nothing else changes. Card details go from the browser straight to Stripe. The session's client secret is kept with the payment so the page need not ask Stripe on every load; only the cart's own browser is shown it. Stripe needs each store's account to have the site's domain registered for Apple Pay, Google Pay, Link and Klarna; Kaizen does this at the first checkout on each domain and records it (`payment_domains`), and a failure only hides those methods. If the cart changes after the order was placed, or the 30 minutes run out, the page asks the shopper to continue again, which replaces the order. |
| D23 | **Every store's Stripe account asks for cards, Klarna, Link and MobilePay.** Kaizen requests these payment capabilities when it creates a store's account (test and live), and for older accounts in the background when the store's admin is opened or a checkout starts; it records what it asked for (`payment_methods_requested`). On the test accounts Kaizen makes, it also switches these on (with Apple Pay and Google Pay) in the account's display settings, which otherwise follow the platform's defaults for connected accounts (`payment_methods_shown`); owners of live accounts choose in their own Stripe Dashboard. Test accounts also carry Stripe's test Norwegian org number, which MobilePay asks for. Each order records the methods Stripe offered (`payment.started`), and each account keeps why a method is not on yet (`requirements`). | 2026-09-24 | Stripe then offers each method where it fits the shopper's country and currency (MobilePay in Denmark and Finland), and the store's own Stripe settings still decide. Swish and Vipps are in private preview at Stripe: Kaizen's platform account must be given access first, and Vipps is not yet available for Accounts v2; they are added to the list once possible. PayPal is not offered: Stripe does not allow it for platforms whose stores take direct charges on their own accounts. |
| D24 | **Every variant is either shipped or downloaded; a product sets the default.** As in Shopify (a per-variant "physical product" flag) and WooCommerce (Virtual and Downloadable), delivery is chosen per variant, so one product can sell a hardcover and an e-book; the editor asks once per product and offers per-variant choice behind a checkbox. Downloads have no stock, weight or customs details, need no shipping and no manufacturer (EU product-safety rules cover physical goods), and must have at least one file before they go on sale. Files are uploaded from the owner's browser straight to a private storage bucket (`digital-files`, one folder per store) and belong to every digital variant of the product or to one of them. When an order is paid, each digital line gets one personal link per file (`order_downloads`), limited by the product's downloads per file (5 by default) and days (30 by default), either of which can be off. The link counts a download in one statement and sends the shopper to a signed storage address that works for 60 seconds. Buying a download needs the shopper's tick at checkout: express consent to delivery straight away and acknowledgement that the right of withdrawal then ends (CRD art. 16(m); angrerettloven § 22 n). The time is kept on the order (`digital_consent_at`) and in its history; digital lines record the `digital_content` withdrawal exclusion and shipped lines never do. | 2026-09-24 | A basket of downloads only has no shipping, and the checkout form asks for no address. Download links show on the order page, which only the shopper has (it needs the Stripe session in its address); there is no order email yet, so it is the only place until emails exist. Files removed from a product stop new sales but keep working for earlier buyers. New stores copy the template's catalogue with each product's delivery, but not its files, so a download in the template arrives as a draft. Subscriptions (the next slice) will be purchase options on a product, as in Shopify's selling plans and WooCommerce's subscription options. |
| D25 | **Subscriptions are purchase options on a product, charged by Stripe Billing on the store's own account.** As Shopify's selling plans and WooCommerce's subscription options: a product gets up to five purchase options (every 1–52 weeks, 1–12 months or 1–3 years, with a subscriber's discount in whole percent), and can be sold only by subscription. Shoppers choose on the product page between buying once and an option; the prices follow. One checkout starts at most one subscription, so a cart holds one schedule (items bought once can join it). The checkout then runs in Stripe's subscription mode, with Kaizen's fee as `application_fee_percent`; the shopper ticks that they agree to the renewal amount and schedule, and that they can cancel any time. Kaizen keeps the subscription and what each renewal holds (`subscriptions`, `subscription_lines`), at the prices agreed at the start. Each paid renewal (`invoice.paid`, `subscription_cycle`) becomes a paid order: stock is drawn and downloads made as for any order, once per invoice. Stripe's subscription events keep the status, next renewal and cancellation in step. Shoppers cancel from a link on their order page, without an account (as easy as subscribing), effective at the end of the paid period, and can take it back; staff can also cancel at once. | 2026-09-24 | Stripe takes no shipping options in subscription mode, so shipping is a line: a subscription with something to ship pays shipping on every delivery, worked out on what each delivery holds (free above the store's threshold), and items bought once travel with the first delivery. Without such a subscription the usual rule applies. Options taken off a product are switched off, not deleted, so carts, orders and subscriptions keep pointing at them. Kaizen's existing webhook for stores' accounts is updated with the subscription events at the first subscription checkout, without replacing it. Stripe sends its own invoice for every charge. Not yet: trials, sign-up fees, pausing, skipping or swapping a delivery, changing quantities, a minimum number of renewals, renewal reminders by email (no emails yet), and Stripe's customer portal. |
| D26 | **Kaizen sends shoppers' emails in the store's name, through Resend (D32).** The sender is Kaizen's verified address with the store's name, and replies go to the store's contact address. Every email is written to `email_messages` before it is sent (who, why, subject, the email itself, and whether it was sent), so staff can read exactly what a shopper got: stores under Orders → Emails to customers, and each order's history; Kaizen under Platform → Emails. Emails are plain HTML with a text version, in the order's language, with the store's legal details at the foot. A key per event (such as `order-confirmation:{order}`) makes each email go once, however often a webhook arrives. | 2026-09-24 | Until `RESEND_API_KEY` and `EMAIL_FROM` are set in Vercel, emails are only recorded (`logged`), and nothing else waits on them. The sending domain must be verified in Resend (D32). Amazon SES was the first plan and was removed unused. The first emails: the order confirmation, for new orders and each subscription renewal, with the download and subscription links. Sign-in codes, shipping, refunds and subscription reminders follow. Stripe's own receipts can stay on as well (R7). |
| D27 | **Staff manage the whole order from its page.** Mark it sent with carrier and tracking number (Posten, Bring, PostNord, DHL, UPS build their tracking link; others take a pasted one), with an email to the customer; more parcels can follow (`shipments`). Refund any amount up to what is left, through Stripe on the store's own account, with Kaizen's fee on the refunded part returned to the store (`refund_application_fee`); choose which items go back in stock, with or without money back; the customer is emailed. Cancel a paid order before it is sent: everything left is refunded, all items go back in stock and download links stop. Correct the customer's email and delivery address, keep notes only staff see, print a packing slip in the customer's language, and send the confirmation again. The history shows every event and every email the customer got. | 2026-09-24 | Refunds of subscription orders refund that payment only; the subscription goes on until cancelled on its page. Orders cancelled after payment stay in the order list, marked "Cancelled and refunded"; a "To send" filter lists paid orders with something to ship. Refunds made directly in Stripe's Dashboard are not yet read back into Kaizen. Items go back to the store's first stock location. |
| D28 | **Shoppers get My account per store, signed in with an emailed code or a password they chose.** The code (six digits, ten minutes, five tries, at most five an hour, stored only as a hash) also proves the address, so every order and subscription placed with it joins the account, and later ones join when paid. After that, the customer can add a password (at least 12 characters, scrypt, ten wrong tries lock it for 15 minutes); codes keep working. Nothing on the sign-in page reveals whether an address has an account. The account shows orders (with tracking, downloads and refunds), subscriptions (managed on their own page), the customer's name, phone and address, the password, and deleting the account. A session is a random token in an httpOnly cookie for the store, of which only a hash is stored; it lasts 60 days. | 2026-09-24 | Guest checkout stays as it is. Deleting an account removes the customer's details, password and sessions; orders stay with the store, as bookkeeping law requires, without the link to an account. The account's address starts as the one the last order went to. Signing in by code needs email to be set up (D26); until then codes are only recorded, so shoppers cannot sign in on a store in production. Checkout does not yet prefill from the account. |
| D29 | **Purchase options can have a free trial, a sign-up fee and a commitment; subscribers pause, skip and change their subscription themselves, and are reminded before they are charged.** A free trial (up to 90 days) charges nothing for what renews until it ends (Stripe's `trial_period_days`), and its first delivery ships free; items bought once in the same checkout pay as usual. A sign-up fee is set per market and charged once with the first order, as its own line. A commitment (up to 24 payments, the first included) means a cancellation takes effect when the last committed payment's period ends (Stripe's `cancel_at`); it counts payments made, so pauses and skips move it. Pausing holds up to three deliveries at a time (Stripe's `pause_collection`, which voids the invoices due meanwhile); skipping is a pause of one; not during a trial or while a payment is failing. Changing contents swaps a line to another variant of the same product and delivery, or changes its quantity, or removes it (one must stay); a swapped line takes today's price with the option's discount, a kept one keeps its price; shipping is worked out again, and Stripe charges the new amounts from the next renewal, with nothing prorated. Every change is confirmed by email. A daily job emails a reminder three days before a trial ends and seven days before renewals of a month or longer, once per charge date. Staff can do all of this from the subscription's page, and also end a subscription at once. | 2026-09-24 | Weekly renewals get no reminder: each renewal's confirmation serves. Options with different trials cannot share a checkout, like options with different schedules. Content changes replace the Stripe subscription's items (products are reused by name). Commitment dates are worked out from Stripe's period end by the calendar, so a month-end renewal can end a few days early. The reminder job needs `CRON_SECRET` in Vercel (Vercel Cron sends it); without it, the route refuses every call and no reminders go out. Reminders, like every email, are only recorded until email is set up (D26). |
| D30 | **Every store has a header and footer its owner edits: a logo, a header menu and a footer menu, in each of the store's languages.** Kept on the store as one JSON value (`stores.navigation`), loaded and cached with the store, so pages make no extra query. A menu link goes to the front page, a product (named by handle, so copies of the template keep working), My account, the cart, or a web address (http(s), or a path in the store); at most 8 header and 12 footer links. A product link left without text takes the product's title. The header stays at the top and slides away while the shopper scrolls down, and comes back on the way up; it holds the logo (or name), the header menu on computers, a country chooser, My account and the cart with its count. On phones a Menu button opens a menu that slides in from the left (a modal dialog: focus stays in it; Escape, tapping outside, choosing a link or swiping it away closes it), and a bar fixed along the bottom (Home, Menu, My account, Cart) slides away while scrolling up, when the header returns, so only one shows. On product pages that bar becomes the price, a variant choice and Add to cart, following the purchase option chosen on the page. The footer shows the business details the law requires on every page, the footer menu and the countries. New stores start with the template's logo and menus. | 2026-09-24 | The logo is uploaded like product pictures (shrunk in the browser, up to 800 px) and shown up to 40 px high; PNG, JPEG or WebP, not SVG, which the browser cannot shrink. Menus are one level deep: there are no collections or content pages to group yet. The phone menu and bottom bar are each rendered in their own Suspense boundary: React counts everything outside boundaries towards a 12.8 kB budget, beyond which a page's content is sent in a block that needs JavaScript to show; keeping these enhancements out keeps product pages readable without it. The motion is off for shoppers who ask for reduced motion. |
| D31 | **Stores have discount codes for shoppers, and Kaizen has discount codes for stores' plans.** A store's code gives a percentage, an amount per market (in its currency) or free shipping; on everything or chosen products; with an optional minimum order per market, start and end (Norwegian time), a total number of uses, and one use per customer. Shoppers type it in the cart, which checks it against the basket exactly as checkout will and says why a code does not apply; checkout checks it again under a row lock, so two orders cannot take a code's last use. A code counts as used by every order that got it and is not cancelled, waiting for payment included; a cancelled checkout gives the use back. The discount is spread over the lines it applies to (a percentage per unit, an amount in proportion) and each line's VAT is on what is paid. Stripe gets it as a one-time coupon on the store's account for that checkout alone, for single payments and subscriptions alike; free shipping on a single payment is simply a lower shipping price. A percentage can also lower every renewal of a subscription: the subscriber's price itself is lowered, for good. Orders, emails, My account and the admin show the discount and the code. Kaizen's codes for plans are a percentage or an amount per plan currency, for the first payment, some months or for good, with an optional expiry and number of uses; each is a coupon and a promotion code in Kaizen's Stripe account (in every mode with keys), and Stripe applies it to the plan's invoices. Owners type one on their Plan page: it applies at once to a running plan, or is saved and used when they choose one (in Stripe Checkout or when an admin assigns a plan). Platform admins make and switch codes on the platform's Discounts page, and can put one on any store's plan. | 2026-09-24 | "Once per customer" needs the shopper signed in to My account: before payment Kaizen does not know who is buying otherwise. Any code can be changed or deleted at any time, used or not: orders keep the code's text and the amounts they got, so changing or deleting a code never changes an order (deleting only unlinks it). Stripe's coupons cannot change, so changing what a platform code gives retires its coupon and promotion code in Stripe and makes new ones under the same code; a plan that already has it keeps the old terms, and a store whose code was still waiting for a plan loses it when the code is deleted. Codes are case-insensitive and stored in capitals; store codes may use Æ, Ø and Å, Kaizen's codes only A–Z (Stripe). Stacking several codes on one order is not offered. Codes typed on Stripe's own checkout page are not offered either; codes are entered in Kaizen only, so Kaizen always knows which code a plan has. |
| D32 | **Shoppers can create an account with a password, on My account or at checkout; an email the store already knows chooses a new password instead. Emails go through Resend.** My account has two tabs, Sign in and Create account (name, email, password of at least 12 characters); a new account is signed in at once and gets a welcome email. At checkout, shoppers who are not signed in can tick Create an account and choose a password; it is kept (hashed) with the unpaid order, and the account opens when the order is paid, with the email, name and address they paid with, and that order. If the email already has an account, or paid orders, no account is made: the shopper is asked to choose a new password, which takes a six-digit code emailed to that address (the same rules as sign-in codes); the code proves the inbox is theirs, so all the email's orders then join the account and every other session ends. At checkout this is said on the order page, with the code form right there. An account made with a password starts with its email unproven: only orders placed while signed in join it, until the customer signs in with a code or chooses a new password, so registering someone else's email shows nothing of theirs. Emails are sent with Resend's API from a domain verified in Resend's EU region (Ireland), with each email's id in Kaizen as the idempotency key, so a retry never sends twice; a busy or failing Resend is tried again briefly, and anything else is marked failed in the email log. Resend reports deliveries, bounces and spam complaints to a signed webhook, and the email log shows them. | 2026-09-24 | Chosen by the owner for the easiest setup, price and API (Amazon SES, first planned in D26, was never configured and is removed). Resend is a US company: allowed by D10 with its DPA and standard contractual clauses; see the residency register. Saying that an email has shopped before tells whoever types it that the address has been used in the store; the owner asked for it, as larger shops do. Registering is not rate-limited per visitor yet. A password chosen at checkout is dropped once the order is paid, whatever the outcome. The order page signs the new account in once, within an hour of payment. |
| D33 | **Stores can email reminders about carts left at checkout, and Kaizen about plans left unpaid.** A store turns them on under Cart reminders and starts with three (after an hour, a day and three days), each editable: when it goes (30 minutes to 30 days after the email was typed), on or off, an optional discount code, and a subject, heading, message and button in each of the store's languages, beside a live preview and a test sent to the staff member. While they are on, checkout keeps the email of a shopper who is not signed in as soon as a valid address is typed, with the cart as ordered; right under the email field it says a reminder may come, with a link to say no (and to undo that). Each reminder shows the cart and its total, and has a button that puts the same cart back in the shopper's browser (with the step's code) and a link to stop reminders, with List-Unsubscribe one-click headers. At most one reminder per cart per run, the latest due, so a late run never sends several; each is claimed before it is sent and keyed, so none goes twice. Reminders stop when the cart is paid, when the same email buys anything, when the shopper opts out, and 30 days after capture; the email and cart are erased on opt-out and 60 days after capture. | D37 | **A function never leaves a database connection half-used.** The app talks to Postgres through node-postgres, which sends a query and its values in one message, one query at a time per connection. postgres.js, used before, sent a query with values in two halves without prepared statements and pipelined queries; through the transaction-mode pooler the second half could reach another Postgres connection once the pooler had handed the first back, so the query waited forever while a Postgres connection sat holding its first half. That was the main cause of pages hanging under load. Also, Vercel freezes a function instance between requests. Frozen in the middle of a query, it left the pooler's connection to Postgres waiting for the rest of it (seen: two such connections held for five minutes); enough of those and every query waits for a free connection, so pages hung on their loading placeholders until the pooler let go. Frozen with connections open, it woke up to dead ones. Now every query asks Vercel (through its `attachDatabasePool`) to keep the instance running until the query is done and its connections have been idle for five seconds and closed. As a safety net, Postgres ends any transaction of the app's role open for a minute, or idle inside a transaction for 30 seconds, so a connection is never held for long. The cached reads pages are built from try once more on a passing error (a timeout, a lost connection), so one hiccup does not fail a page or a build. | 2026-09-25 | After pages intermittently hung on "Loading …" in stores and the admin, and a build failed on a timed-out read. The app's transactions take milliseconds and call no outside service, so the limits never cut a real one. |

FAQs (`faq`) are questions and answers drawn as the accordion is, a question shown once it has an answer (`faqShows()`), with schema.org's FAQPage (`faqJsonLd()`) beside them unless switched off, for search engines and AI assistants. A video (`video`) is one uploaded to the site (`VideoUploadButton`, played by the browser with or without its controls; one that starts by itself starts muted, loops, and stays still for visitors who prefer less motion) or one on YouTube or Vimeo, given by its share address (`embedUrl()`, `src/lib/video-embed.ts`). An outside video is a facade until pressed: its poster (a picture from the site, never fetched from YouTube or Vimeo) or a plain panel, a play button saying where it plays from, and only then the player, from youtube-nocookie.com or Vimeo with `dnt=1`, so nothing reaches either before the visitor chooses to play and no consent is needed. Its code is the same in every language; only its title, naming the frame, is translated, and none of its words are the page's. Testimonials (`testimonials`) are what customers said, written in by the owner (words, name, title or place, 1–5 stars, a picture), drawn by `TestimonialCards` as cards, plain or large quotes in one to four columns (one on phones): each a `figure` whose `blockquote` is what was said and whose caption is who said it, the stars read out as words (`StarRating`). The phase 0 spike proved this locally (+0.5 to 0.9 ms) and found that a browser's cached copy goes stale after assignment (a page marker and one reload fix it) and that a dynamic hole flickers; the check on Vercel's network and the proxy's region are still open; one running test per target; variants locked once running; one goal per test, verdict only after the planned minimum, said in plain language with an estimate of the runtime before launch. Phase 1 is built (`docs/ab-testing.md`, "What phase 1 built"): the engine, tests of whole store pages, the admin at `/admin/{store}/experiments`, the proxy, results computed on read and the guardrail job; versions are pages of type `variant`, a page in a running test cannot be unpublished or have a change published, and the migration is `ab_experiments`. Phase 2 adds tests of a part of a page (a row, column or component chosen in the builder with "A/B test this"; a version may differ from the original in that part only, and applying a winner puts only the part into the page as it is then) and a scheduled start, the migration `ab_part_tests`. Phase 3 adds tests of a store's header, footer and product layouts: a visitor's versions travel in the market part of the address the proxy rewrites to (`no~{test}{version}`, taken off again by `resolveShop()`), so every page and the product pages are served from the same routes, and the migration is `ab_site_tests`. Phase 4 adds the AI manager's seven A/B test tools (list, explain, suggest, draft, start, stop, apply): the model words and drafts, code counts and decides, the three that change what visitors see are kept for the owner's yes and checked first; no migration. Phase 5 adds the platform's read-only view of every store's tests at `/admin/platform/experiments`, with the ones that need a look first (a version lowering orders, an uneven split, nobody seeing a running test, a test past its end or left undecided); no migration. Phase 6 emails the store's owners, and whoever made the test, once each when the guardrail stops a test, with the counted figures and what they may do; no migration. Phase 7 moves the search test (D77) and the recommendations held-out ranking (D140) onto the engine's arithmetic (`src/lib/experiment-units.ts`: the same comparison of rates, split check and rule for calling a difference, the old formulas kept in `experiment-legacy.ts` and checked to give the same numbers on the same data) and lists them beside page tests in the platform's view; they keep their units (a search, a tab), their own logs and no cookie, and make no experiment row, so no migration. Phase 8 gives the platform's AI manager two read-only tools over every store's tests (`list_ab_tests`, `explain_ab_test`), with a playbook; it has no tool that starts, stops or changes a store's test, since a platform admin cannot, and says what to tell the owner instead; no migration. Phase 9 lets a store test a modal (a popup that opens by itself may be left out of a version, to see whether it helps; every modal keeps its address name) and the rows around the shop's own component on its working pages (cart, checkout, order confirmation, My account, sign-in, wishlists, a subscription, weekly deliveries: by a part only, served from the page's own route like a header's, the shop's logic never varied); the migration is `ab_working_pages`. Phase 10 makes the store's front page and All products page testable, whole or by a part, served from their own routes like a working page and held in place while a test runs (`commerce.page_place()`, migration `ab_front_pages`); a part test compares the original as it would be saved, since saving keeps only the store's own languages. Phase 11 adds the goal "more people sending a form" (`form`, an email form or newsletter sign-up chosen on the page, counted once per visitor in their version when the site accepts the answer: `recordFormSent()` from `submitForm()`; migration `ab_form_goal`). |

Known limits: VIES says a number is registered, not whose it is, so a private buyer who types a company and someone else's valid number is not charged VAT (staff see a flag on the order); the VIES budget per store and hour can be used up by many carts. Documents are frozen JSON snapshots, immutable except a one-time `pdf_path` and `anonymise_expired_documents()` (unit 1g's hook, 5-year floor), with no delete and no direct insert. All consumer wording is hand-written nb, sv, da, en and needs legal review. Rows: `orders.invoices-and-vat-receipts-for-orders`, `orders.credit-notes-for-refunds`, `international.legal-invoices-and-credit-notes-for-orders`, held at Partial until the wording is reviewed and a real PDF is read per country. *Why:* the largest weighted gap after returns; draft orders, order editing, gift cards, payouts and unit 1c all need correct documents. | D160 | **Unit price indication: the price per kilogram, litre or metre beside the price.** A goods variant carries a total measure (g, kg, ml, cl, l, cm, m, m2, piece) and the owner's preferred comparison base (`product_variants.measure_amount/measure_unit/measure_base`). The shop shows the price per measure on the product page (following the chosen variant and purchase option), listing cards (for the variant the card's price shows), the cart and slide-out cart, checkout, the order page, the order emails, the chat's product cards, and the subscription and weekly-delivery lists. The product's JSON-LD carries an `Offer.priceSpecification` (`UnitPriceSpecification` with `referenceQuantity` and `valueReference`); `unitPricingMeasure` is a Merchant Center feed name, not schema.org, and waits for the feed in wave 5. The figure is only ever worked out by `unitPrice()` (`src/lib/unit-price.ts`: integers, half up to the minor unit) from the price as shown. A euro view or a business buyer's net price therefore gets its own figure, never a converted one (435 cents for 250 g is 1740 per kg, where converting the krone figure would give 1739). It is omitted when it equals the price or the price is 0, and it never changes a total: it is display plus a frozen snapshot on the order line (`order_lines.measure_*`, copied by `placeOrder()`, the subscription renewal and `copy_orders()`). A product marked `sold_by_measure`, or in a product category marked `requires_unit_price` (or under a marked ancestor), cannot be saved active while an active physical variant has no measure (`commerce.unit_price_required()` plus a deferred constraint trigger); existing products are grandfathered and reported (`productsNeedingMeasure()`). | D237 | **Shipping methods, zones and profiles, local pickup and local delivery (wave 3).** `docs/wave-3-shipping-methods.md` is the contract. **Methods, zones and profiles.** Per market, named methods (`shipping_methods`) carry rates per zone and profile (`shipping_method_rates`). A rate is flat, by basket weight or by basket value. Tiers run from an inclusive minimum to an exclusive maximum with no gap, held by the deferred trigger `shipping_rates_tiers`. Zones are postal codes and prefixes inside a country (`shipping_zones`); the most specific pattern wins and Rest of country takes the rest. Profiles group products (`shipping_profiles`), with General for the rest. A mixed basket is offered a method only when every profile has a matching tier, and pays their sum, free above the method's value. Goods without a weight weigh the store's default per unit (`shipping_settings`, 500 g). **Flat rate.** The market's flat rate stays as the fallback when no method prices a basket. It is the only shipping of subscriptions, weekly boxes (`placeOrder({ flatRateOnly })`) and drafts. **Pickup and local delivery.** Pickup is set per place (`pickup_options`: price, ready time, instructions). Local delivery is set per area (`local_delivery_areas`), by postal codes or by a radius from a place measured between GeoNames postal-code centres (`postal_points`, CC BY 4.0, NO/SE/DK/FI). An area has a price, a minimum and a free-above value, and the cheapest matching area is offered. **Cart and order.** The cart holds one choice and the postal code. `chosenDelivery()` stays the one reader for `cartSummary()` and `placeOrder()` and re-prices the store's own methods on every read. Orders keep `delivery_method`, a snapshot in `delivery`, the place and the driver's note. **Handovers.** *Ready for pickup* emails once (`order-ready:{id}`). *Collected* records a handover (`shipments.method = 'pickup'`) and `delivered_at` together; *Out for delivery* records a `local` handover. | D294 | **Nested columns, one level deep.** A column can hold a *Columns* component (the Components tab's *Columns*, two columns to start), whose columns are columns like a row's, with their own settings, lines and widths; a nested column holds any component but another Columns. The owner switches each tool off, `read` (runs at once) or behind a gate (`public`, `send`, `spend`). The AI manager offers the tools switched on (at most `APP_TOOLS_OFFERED` 20, beside its own within `TOOLS_PER_TURN`) to owners only and never in an autopilot step, named `app__{app}__{tool}` (`appToolName()`), described as the owner's own app's words; a gated call is kept as any gated tool is (`keepForApproval()`, its summary naming the app, the tool and its arguments) and run by `decideApproval()` only while the person is still an owner and the tool still on with a gate. Each call (`callAppTool()`, `tools/call` with the model's arguments as an object) is counted on the app (`calls`, `failed`, `last_called_at`) and logged, and its answer reaches the model as text only (`toolAnswerText()`: other kinds named, cut to 8,000 characters) beside the rule that it is data from outside (`UNTRUSTED_TEXT`). Calls are counted on the app, not as `custom_app` in `ai_usage` as section 3 said: a tool call has no model, tokens or price, and an unpriced row would stop the autopilot's budget (`aiBudgetProblem()`). `safeFetch()`'s answer now carries the response's headers. `ai.third-party-apps-extend-the-assistant` moves to full. Migration versions: `20261028142058_custom_apps` (applied by CI on 28 October 2026, run 702; advisors to check). |
| D364 | **Refund to store credit (wave 10 unit A, `docs/wave-10-must-haves.md` 2); built.** Staff choose *Refund to: the original payment / store credit* in an order's refund form. A store credit refund asks no provider: `refundOrder({ toCredit })` splits the amount over the order's captured payments as any refund (`splitRefund()`, so the card can later be refunded only what is left) and records each part as a refund of kind `store_credit` (`REFUND_KINDS`; created `succeeded`, never an exchange's or a change's, capped by the database like money taken outside, `refunds_manual_cap()`); a gift card's own part still goes back on that card. In the same transaction the database issues ONE gift card for the credit (`commerce.gift_card_issue_refund()`: source `refund`, `gift_cards.refund_id`, the order's currency and mode, for the order's customer and address, its expiry from the store's settings, once per refund), its code set and the card delivered; after the commit the code is emailed to the order's own address (`sendRefundCredit()`, `gift_card.issued`, the code a secret of the email log) and shown once to the staff member. It is a refund everywhere a refund counts (its credit note, sales, bonus and referral reversals); Kaizena Flow's fee is not returned, as Stripe is not asked. Refused for an amount of zero, a host's booking and any caller's own transaction, exchange or payment. Words: `giftCardEmail.refundSubject`/`refundText` (nb, sv, da, en, `HAND_WRITTEN_ONLY` with the gift card email), the `order` catalogue's `refundTo*` and `credit*`. `orders.partial-and-full-refunds-with-restocking` moves to full. Migration versions: `20261028151057_store_credit_refunds`, `20261028151136_store_credit_refunds_rules` (applied by CI; the release job of run 710 found nothing left pending). |

Accounts cannot be switched off while subscriptions, the bonus programme or referrals are on or a company account buys in the store, and those features cannot be switched on while accounts are off (`setFeature()`). `checkout.guest-checkout-and-optional-account` moves to full. ### Selling from Norway to Sweden and Denmark

Norway is in the EEA but outside the EU's customs and VAT union, so a Norwegian
company shipping from Norway sells to Swedish and Danish customers as an
exporter. In practice:

- **Norwegian VAT (MVA).** Register once sales in Norway pass NOK 50,000 in 12
  months, and charge Norwegian VAT on Norwegian orders.
- **EU VAT on low-value parcels.** For orders worth up to €150, the store can
  register for the EU's Import One-Stop Shop (IOSS) and charge Swedish or
  Danish VAT (25% for standard goods) at checkout. Parcels then clear customs
  without the customer paying anything on delivery. To confirm with an
  accountant: Norway's VAT cooperation agreement with the EU is understood to let
  Norwegian companies register for IOSS without an EU intermediary.
- **Without IOSS**, the carrier collects VAT plus a handling fee from the
  customer on delivery. That is legal but a known reason for refused parcels
  and lost repeat customers.
- **EU customs duty.** Since 1 July 2026 the EU charges a flat €3 duty per item
  category on low-value parcels, which IOSS does not collect. Orders over €150
  pay normal duty and import VAT. The store should show these costs at checkout
  or ship duties-paid.
- **Customs declarations.** Every parcel needs a Norwegian export and an EU
  import declaration, normally filed by the carrier (Posten/Bring, PostNord)
  from the tariff code and country of origin now stored per variant.
- **Later option: stock in the EU.** With a warehouse in Sweden, EU sales
  become domestic and intra-EU: no customs per parcel, but a Swedish VAT
  registration and the EU One-Stop Shop. Worth reconsidering as EU volume grows.
- **Consumer law.** Norwegian customers are covered by angrerettloven and
  forbrukerkjøpsloven (complaints up to five years for goods meant to last).
  Swedish and Danish customers are covered by EU consumer law, including the
  withdrawal button and the 30-day prior-price rule. The store follows the
  stricter rule wherever the two differ.
- **Product safety.** Products sold to Swedish and Danish consumers fall under
  the EU General Product Safety Regulation, which needs an EU-based responsible
  person when the manufacturer is not in the EU. Norway is not in the EU for
  this purpose unless the regulation has been taken into the EEA Agreement
  (unverified).
- **To verify with Stripe:** that Stripe Tax covers Norwegian VAT and IOSS, and
  that Vipps MobilePay is available.

The template store was seeded from `supabase/seed.sql`, and the existing owner
account was carried over as platform admin and owner of the template store.

Supabase records each migration with the version it was applied at, not the
timestamp in the file name. This does not matter while migrations are applied
through Supabase's API. If the Supabase CLI is adopted later (for example for
branching), run `supabase migration repair` once to align the history.
| D366 | **Customers in the admin: added and changed by staff, notes, a tag filter, merging two, and a customer import (wave 10 unit C, `docs/wave-10-must-haves.md` 4); built.** Staff with `customers:write` add a customer (`/customers/new`) and change one's name, email, phone, address and company (the customer page's *Edit details*) through the one writer `src/server/customer-staff.ts` (`createCustomerIn()`/`updateCustomerIn()`, the form's fields checked by `cleanCustomerInput()` in `src/lib/customer-staff.ts`, shared with the import): an account with no password and an email not proven (the person signs in with a code, D32; nothing is emailed and nobody is subscribed), an email another customer of the store has is refused (`taken`), a changed email is unproven again and the person's tags and notes move with it, the address is the default saved one (D304), a company needs its name and a valid organisation number, and a refusal found after a write undoes the transaction. A guest is given an account by their own address (`addGuestAsCustomer()`). Notes are `commerce.customer_notes` (by the store and the person's address, with author and time, never edited by a database rule, deleted by staff; personal data: export, erasure, `PERSONAL_DATA`, `never` in `COPY_RULES`); the activity log keeps a note's id and length, never its words, and a customer's change as `{ changed: true }` per field. The list filters by tag (`?tag=`, `listCustomers({ tag })`). A merge (`src/server/customer-merge.ts`, `/customers/{id}/merge`) folds another account into the one kept by the email staff type: orders (copied ones only lose the account), subscriptions, cancelled subscription box lists, open drafts, carts, wishlists, saved addresses, support conversations, Work clients, codes named for the customer, custom field values the kept one lacks, tags, notes and the bonus balance (one entry granted to the kept account; the removed account's ledger is deleted with it, as an erasure's is, so a taking entry would lose its allocations before the ledger's check at commit) move, then the other account is deleted (its sessions, back-in-stock requests and buyer roles at a company location go with it); it is refused before anything changes, with the reason staff read (`MERGE_REFUSALS`), for a company the kept one is not in, subscription box lists not cancelled, reviews, gift cards, the referral program, credits still pending, or more addresses or tags than one person may hold; the preview runs the same plan in a transaction it rolls back, and the merge reads it again under both rows' locks. The owner imports customers (`/customers/import`, a D165 job `customer_import`, the stock import's pipeline: dry run, per-row findings that name a column and never quote a cell, a problems CSV, resumable): our own customer file or Shopify's (`readHeader()` in `src/lib/customer-import.ts`), a row finding its customer by email, an empty cell keeping what the store has, tags added, never a password set and never anyone subscribed (marketing and password columns are noted and not read), each row its own transaction through the staff writer. Words are the `customers` catalogue's `staff` (en, nb), the import's shared words the `inventory` catalogue's. The admin-strings scan no longer reads the `>` of `=> Promise<…>` as a tag (its baseline shrank). `customers.customer-profiles-notes-csv-import-and-export` moves to full. Migration versions: `20261028183302_customer_admin`, `20261028183325_customer_admin_rules` (applied by CI, run 713). |
| D367 | **Discount combinations between campaigns and codes (wave 10 unit D, `docs/wave-10-must-haves.md` section 4, D); built.** An owner says whether a campaign combines with discount codes (`campaigns.combines_with_codes`, the campaign editor's *Can be used with discount codes*) and whether a code combines with campaigns (`discount_codes.combines_with_campaigns`, the code editor's *Can be used with campaigns*, beside its combinations with other codes of D299 E2); both are on by default, so every existing campaign and code behaves as before (campaigns first, codes count what they leave). Where they do not combine, the basket takes whichever saves the shopper more, decided once by `campaignsAndCodes()` (`src/server/discount-combinations.ts`, pure rules in `src/lib/discount-combinations.ts`) for `cartSummary()` and `placeOrder()` alike: (a) every campaign, with the codes they let in (`codeRuleFor()`: `any` while no campaign gives the basket anything, `combining` while every campaign that gives combines with codes, `none` once one does not), or (b) the codes as they would be used with no campaign, with only the campaigns that combine with codes, or none at all when a code used does not combine with campaigns (`evaluateCampaigns()`' `leaveOut`). The saving counts the campaigns' lines, a free product's worth and shipping made free, the codes (shipping included) and what the group's discount (D108) and the friend's welcome discount (D131) then take, each by the caller's own arithmetic (`AfterCampaigns`); the codes win only when strictly more and a code is used at all (`codesWin()`), a tie keeps the campaigns. The alternatives are evaluated only when a code on the cart is kept out by the campaigns, so a basket without such a conflict costs one evaluation as before. The group's discount, the welcome discount and bonus credits keep their order (after the campaigns, before the codes; credits last); `placeOrder()` now reads the basket's delivery, the group's discount and the friend's state before the campaigns, so a checkout rule's refusal, unanswered questions or no shipping are said before a stock problem. The loser is said, never hidden: a code kept out is refused as `with_campaigns` (`m.codeProblems.with_campaigns`, never `alone`, so it does not stop the checkout), a campaign left out is `cartSummary().campaignsLeftOut`, said in the cart with `m.campaignNotWithCode` (both by hand in nb, sv, da and en). At checkout a code typed on the waiting order is let through when only the order's campaigns keep it out (`checkCodeForOrder()`), since placing the order again weighs it, and the order's codes are shown with the rule its campaigns set (`stackOnOrder()`, from the lines' `campaign_parts` and `campaign_shipping`). The AI manager's `create_campaign` and `create_discount` take `combines_with_codes` and `combines_with_campaigns` (on unless said; the approval names it), and `list_campaigns`/`list_discounts` say which do not. A store's copy carries both (`duplicate_store()` patched in place); `clone_store()` copies no campaigns or codes. Scenarios in `checkout-kinds.int.test.ts`, in kroner and shown in euro: a non-combining code where the campaign gives more, where the code gives more, a campaign that does not combine with a combining code that gives more (a combining free product staying), both combining, and a non-combining campaign that gives more for a group member; cart and order agree to the minor unit and the order keeps the code only when the cart used it. `customers.automatic-discounts` moves to full. Migrations: `20261028172238_discount_combinations`, `20261028172302_discount_combinations_copy` (applied by CI; the release job of run 710 found nothing left pending). |
| D370 | **Inventory: the export's `on_hand_was`, a first alert for a new variant, the pages in a browser (wave 10 unit G, `docs/wave-10-must-haves.md` 4); built.** The stock export writes `on_hand_was` (the stock it was made from), so a file counted from an export and brought back is checked against it and a row whose stock moved since is a conflict, as the import already read the column. A variant created at or below its low-stock level, or given a level it is already at or below (`off` to `low`), is a crossing at once: `nextAlertState()` and `commerce.refresh_stock_alert()` still write such a crossing with `notified_at` equal to `crossed_at` (the same transaction's instant), and the job reads that, or null, as not yet told (`untold()`, `UNTOLD_SQL`), tells it once and marks it with its own time. The 20-line order guard's flakiness had a cause: after other tests had made many small stores, the planner's statistics gave the store one variant and one product and scanned every variant per product; the cart page's read and `placeOrder()` now take the cart's lines first (`cartLinesFirst()` in `cart.ts`), and `inventory-perf.int.test.ts` times the cart page's read too. `e2e/signed-in/inventory.spec.ts` opens the Inventory page, reviews and saves a counted figure with its reason, follows it into the variant's history and makes a stock file. `catalogue.inventory-tracking-with-reservations` moves to full. No migration. |

| D372 | **Partial fulfilment with a carrier, and a second parcel of the same order booked straight after the first (wave 10 unit I, `docs/wave-10-must-haves.md` 4); built.** The refusal "This order was just booked with Bring" was Kaizena Flow's own: `bringBook()`, `helthjemBook()` and `porterbuddyBook()` each refused any booking of an order that had a parcel of that carrier from the last two minutes, a double-click guard (D134) that also refused the second parcel of a partly sent order. Bring never refused one: its Booking request (`bookingBody()`) carries nothing of the order (no reference, no correlation id), so there was nothing of Bring's to make unique. The window is gone, replaced by what every carrier booking now shares (`src/server/carrier-booking.ts`): one booking of an order at a time, under a transaction-scoped advisory lock taken without waiting (`oneBookingAtATime()`, `carrier-book:{order}`; a second booking while the first is with the carrier is told *Another booking of this order is being made right now*, `BOOKING_BUSY`), the parcel checked under the lock before the carrier is asked or paid (`bookingPrecheck()`: `parcelPrecheck()`, and with `seen`, the order's fulfilment as the page showed it, `OrderFulfilment.basis`, a press made before the page showed the last parcel is refused as `changed`), then `markSent()` with the parcel's lines as before. The order page's three booking forms send `seen` (`BringBooking`, `ChosenDeliveryBooking`, `basis`). Reading the carriers' requests found the real cause of the same failure elsewhere: Porterbuddy's booking sent the order's number as its `Idempotency-Key`, so Porterbuddy would have answered a second parcel of the order with the first parcel's booking. A booking now carries `BookingRequest.parcelReference` (`parcelReference()`: the order's number for its first parcel, `{number}-{n}` for the n-th, undone parcels counted, read under the lock so a retry of a failed booking keeps its key), which Porterbuddy's adapter sends as the key; Helthjem's `reference` stays the order's number (it is a reference, not a key). Integration tests book part of an order with each carrier (a parcel naming only its lines and units, the order `paid` and *Partly sent* after it, the rest booked straight after as its own parcel and the order sent, a stale `seen` refused before the carrier is asked, nothing left to send refused before the carrier is asked; Bring also two bookings at once, the second told to wait; Porterbuddy each parcel's own key against a fake that answers a repeated key as Porterbuddy does): `bring-shipping.int.test.ts`, `helthjem-shipping.int.test.ts`, `porterbuddy-shipping.int.test.ts`. **Objectives (REL-09, 30 October 2026):** each part has a service level objective over the last 30 days, worked out from the same checks (`SLO_TARGETS`, `sloOf()`): 99.9 % for stores and websites, sign-in and payments, 99.5 % for email and background work (which retry by themselves); the page shows the share measured, met or missed, and the minutes of failed checks still allowed (a check every five minutes, `CHECK_MINUTES`). | 2026-10-28 | The parity row's gap named two things: no carrier booking of part of an order was tested, and two Bring parcels of one order could not be booked back to back. The spec said a second booking "waits and retries"; there was nothing at Bring to wait for, so the guard that caused it was replaced instead, keeping what it was for (no parcel paid for twice by a double press or a second tab). No migration. |
| D373 | **Express checkout on the product page and in the cart, wallets per web address, Klarna's line (wave 10 unit J, `docs/wave-10-must-haves.md` 4); built.** The express area (`ExpressArea`, `src/components/express-area.tsx`) is a plain button until it is pressed, so nothing of Stripe's is in a product page's first scripts: the press calls `expressCheckoutAction()` (in the cart's actions), which on a product page first puts the chosen variant in the cart through `addToCart()` itself, then `startExpress()` (`src/server/express-checkout.ts`): the basket must be goods sent by post and bought once (`expressFits()` in `src/lib/express-checkout.ts`: a download needs the shopper's tick, a subscription its consent, a booking its time and contact, a gift card who it is for, a host's listing the host's account, which a wallet's sheet cannot ask), the delivery must be settled without a postal code the wallet would give only later (`deliveryReady()`), and then the order is placed and its Checkout Session opened by `startCheckout()`, the cart button's own path, so price, VAT, stock held, discounts and the delivery are decided once; the open checkout's client secret goes to the browser that owns the cart, as on the checkout page. Only then is `express-panel.tsx` loaded (Stripe's Express Checkout Element over `CheckoutElementsProvider`), whose wallet press runs the checkout page's steps (`deliveryReadyAction()`, the store's terms recorded and held while a box is unticked) before `checkout.confirm()`; Stripe returns the shopper to the order page, and the wallet's address and the cart's delivery reach the order through `applySession()` as for any payment. It is offered only where `expressOn()` says (Kaizena Flow's own checkout page, Stripe as the store's checkout, payments on, not a store template, a signed-in shopper where accounts are required (D365), a private buyer, no checkout questions (D357)), on a product of goods or a bundle without purchase options, for its variants sent by post and in stock, and in a cart that fits; a product page's press pays for the whole cart and the panel says so when the cart holds more. Klarna's line under a price (`KlarnaMessage`, Stripe's messaging element, `klarna-element.tsx`) loads once the price is on the screen and the browser is idle, only where `klarnaMessaging()` finds Klarna active on the store's account in the mode it takes payments in, on for the country (D291), and a currency and country the element draws. The Payments page's *Wallets and express checkout* card (`WalletsCard`) lists Apple Pay, Google Pay, Link and Klarna with their capability on the account and their state on each web address the store's shoppers pay on (`walletHosts()`: its own hosts once it has them, else Kaizena Flow's) as Stripe's `PaymentMethodDomain` reports it, with Stripe's reason; *Check again* (owners, `checkWalletDomains()`) registers any address missing and reads them back into `stripe_accounts.wallet_domains`. `docs/pci.md` says what the elements on a page outside the pay routes take and do not take. Held by `express-checkout.int.test.ts` (a fake Stripe: the express press places the cart's order through checkout with the chosen shipping method as the session's option, the wallet's sheet completes it, and the order is paid with the wallet's address and that delivery; refused with an empty cart before anything is placed; not offered where an account is required; Klarna's line only while active and on for the country; each address registered and its wallets' states kept with Stripe's reason) and `express-checkout.test.ts`. `checkout.accelerated-checkout-apple-pay-google-pay-shop-pay` and `checkout.klarna` move to full. | 2026-10-28 | The parity rows' criteria: express buttons beyond the checkout page through the existing checkout, each wallet and address's state, Klarna's messaging. A product page's express payment buys the whole cart rather than a cart of its own: a second cart would need a second cookie and a second checkout path, which the rule of one path for every order forbids. Migration: `20261028210055_express_wallets` (two columns on `stripe_accounts`; applied by CI, run 715). |

| D423 | **Leaving a page in Safari goes where the visitor asked.** Next.js's router fetches a page's data and, when that request fails for any reason but its own cancel, loads the page's address in full (`fetchServerResponse()`, `next/dist/.../router-reducer/fetch-server-response.js`). Safari's engine cancels a page's requests the moment a whole-page load starts (`beforeunload` fires, then the requests fail with *Load failed*), before `pagehide` and while the page's scripts still run, so a visitor who left a page while the router was still fetching the next one (an address typed, a bookmark, a plain link, a form) was taken to the page being fetched instead. CI's WebKit search test met it (run #891, both tries), and so did 6 of 70 runs of it locally. `patches/next.patch` (`patchedDependencies` in `pnpm-workspace.yaml`, for any version of Next.js): while a router request is out, a `beforeunload` listener notes the time; a request that fails within three seconds of it, or after `pagehide`, waits instead of falling back; if the visitor comes back to the page from the back-forward cache (`pageshow`), it is answered with a fresh load of the page as it stands, the address they came back to, never the one it was on its way to. `e2e/store-pages.spec.ts` holds the search page's request and leaves by a whole-page load: WebKit failed it every time before the patch. | 2026-11-02 | *Why a patch, not app code:* the decision to load the page is made inside the router, and a wrapper around `fetch` would not see a failure while the response body streams. Next.js 16.4.4 and 16.5's canary still fall back the same way (checked 2 November 2026). *Why the listener only while a request is out:* a standing `beforeunload` listener can keep a page out of the back-forward cache. *Why three seconds:* the cancel comes within milliseconds of `beforeunload`; a leave called off at an admin editor's *leave this page?* prompt must not keep a later real failure from falling back. *On a Next.js upgrade:* the patch goes with it while the lines it changes are the same (16.4.4's are); where they change, pnpm refuses the install until the patch is moved, or dropped once Next.js stops falling back on a cancel; the test says which. First kept for 16.4.2 alone, which stopped Dependabot's Next.js updates (its run of 2 November failed on `next`); keyed by name the same day. |

| D429 | **Prices with or without decimals, and the owner's words around a product's price.** A store chooses whether whole amounts show their decimals (`stores.price_decimals`: `always`, the default and what every store had, or `hide_whole`: 499 kr, while 499,50 kr keeps its decimals), and each country may differ (`markets.price_decimals`, null for the store's). It is never a rounding: `formatMoney(minor, currency, locale, style)` leaves off only zeros, so what is shown is what is charged. Every amount a shopper sees follows the market's style (`Market.priceStyle`, built by `localized()` from the store's row): product pages, cards and grids, search, the phone's bar, the cart, checkout, the account pages, the chat's cards and answers, and the store's emails to shoppers (with the notifications' preview); invoices, credit notes, UBL, tax reports, feeds and the admin keep their decimals. A word is at most 24 characters of plain text with no percentage and nothing `findClaims()` finds (`priceWordProblem()`, checked in the browser, by the server and, for length and tags, by the database). One settings page, *Prices and quantity* (`/admin/{store}/settings/prices`): Homer's decimals and the main language's words with a preview; each country's decimals and the other languages' words in the Advanced fold; a product's own words in its editor's Advanced fold. A store copy (D129) and a store made from a template (D175) bring the settings and a product's words. Migrations: `20261103005650_price_display` and `20261103013420_price_display_copy` (custom: `duplicate_store()` and `clone_starter_setup()` copy the new columns; `20261103022656_price_words_template_copy`, with D431, makes `clone_store()` carry a product's words too). | D436 | **New interface text reaches the machine-translated languages by itself.** Once a night the platform's AI (`aiFor(null, { feature: 'ui_translation' })`, Kaizena Flow's own key) translates the interface texts each kept-up language has none for yet: a language switched on in `commerce.platform_languages`, not written by hand (nb, sv, da, en never are), that already has interface text, which a platform admin gave it with *Translate* on Platform → Languages (D111). | D443 | **The docs' search and filters (wave 14 unit E3, `docs/wave-14-developer-platform.md` E3); built.** *The index:* `commerce.docs_index` (SQL only, as `knowledge_chunks`: its vector is a type of another schema; RLS on, no policy) holds one row per part of an article (its start, the summary and the words before the first heading, then each `##` and `###` with the words below it, a `####` staying in its part) and of the changelog, and one per reference item of unit A's contracts (each `ADMIN_API` operation, `WEBHOOK_TOPICS` topic, owner MCP tool, shopping agent's tool, error code and Admin API scope, `src/lib/docs-reference.ts`): track, kind, item, areas, features, plans, language, section, the address with its anchor, title, headings, code, summary and words, a `tsvector` stemmed by the row's language through `commerce.search_config()` (english, norwegian; the title weighs A, headings and code B, words C), the same unstemmed (`words`, for a word's start while it is typed), trigram text of the title, headings and code (`trgm`, pg_trgm, already in `extensions`; a GIN `gin_trgm_ops` index) and an embedding with its model's `space`, as the chat's knowledge (D81). `docsIndexRows()` (`src/lib/docs-index.ts`, pure) makes the rows from the compiled docs and the contracts; `refreshDocsIndex()` (`src/server/docs-search.ts`), in the five-minute dispatcher (`docsIndex`), compares the sha256 of their fingerprint with `commerce.docs_index_state` and rewrites the index in one transaction under an advisory lock when it moved (after a deploy that changed an article, a contract or how rows are made), keeping a row's vector while its words (`text_hash`) are the same and removing the rows no longer made; then it gives up to 256 rows a run vectors from the platform's AI (AI feature `docs_search`) while it has an embedding model. The answer says how the words matched, whether meaning took part, how many documents the words found before the filters (`found`) and after (`total`). *On the page:* the top bar's search is a link to the search page until its script runs, then a button opening a `<dialog>` as a modal (⌘K, Ctrl+K and `/` say `DOCS_SEARCH_EVENT`): it searches as the reader types (200 ms), starts within the page's language and, on a track's page, that track (two chips, one press each to take away), shows *For* and *Language* with their counts and the kinds, topics and orders under *More filters*, each result with its track, section (or what kind of reference item) and heading, its code, its words with the search's marked (text, never HTML) and its kind; ↓ from the field to the results, ↑ and ↓ between them, Enter opens one (in the field, the first), typing goes back to the field, Esc, the close button or a click outside closes it and the focus goes back; the count is said politely. `/docs/search` (`/search` and `/no/search` on the docs' host, `docsHostRoutes()`) draws the same panel with the search done on the server (`instant = false`: no static shell and no streamed part, which would need a script to show), so it works without JavaScript: the form submits there with its filters, and every chip, order and *Show more* is a link there, which a plain click with JavaScript follows in place (keeping the address in step). The dialog's *Open this search as a page* is the address to share. `noindex`, and disallowed in the docs' host's `robots.txt`. A section's page lists its kinds and topics with their counts and the four orders as links to the search page with the section as a filter (`DocsSectionFilters`, counted at build by the same `facetCounts()`), so a section stays prerendered. A search that finds nothing offers the whole docs when filters hid it, else tips, says it is counted, and offers the AI guide with the question filled in only once the guide exists: the hand-over is `DOCS_ASK_EVENT` with `{ question }` in the dialog and `/docs?ask=…` (`docsAskSub()`) on the page, shown while `DOCS_GUIDE_READY`, which unit E5 sets. The first search after the deploy filled the index (346 English rows, 9 Norwegian), and the dispatcher's `docsIndex` job adds their vectors. | 2026-11-03 | *Why the index is rows made from code and a fingerprint, not a build step:* the deployed files and contracts are the build's, the cron already runs every five minutes and reads them at no cost, and a fingerprint of the rows themselves moves with any change to an article, a contract or the way rows are made, so nothing has to remember to rebuild it. *Why the API has no same-site rule:* it is a read that changes nothing, as the neighbouring public reads (the domain search, D315; *Show more reviews*; the storefront and shopping agents' APIs) have none, and the docs are meant to be searched by tools (E5's guide, AI tools reading `llms.txt`); what writes (misses, reads) is a POST of its own that is same-site. *Why `docs_search` fails closed:* each search may ask the platform's AI for its words' vector, which costs money, so a counter that cannot count must not let searches through unmetered (`report`'s reason). *Why misses are counted by the dialog after a pause, not by the API:* a word half typed is not a gap, and a GET that writes would count every keystroke and every prefetch. *Why a section's filters are links to the search page:* the section stays prerendered, its filtered list is an address to share and the page works without JavaScript; the counts are the search's own. *Why the guide's offer waits for E5:* an offer that leads nowhere is worse than none; the hand-over is in place for E5 to switch on. *Why no new dependency:* Postgres's text search, pg_trgm and pgvector are already the store search's and the chat's; the dialog is the platform's `<dialog>`. |

| D463 | **E-invoices through Peppol, the parts that need no vendor (B1 of `docs/own-books-and-sales.md`; `src/lib/peppol.ts`, `src/lib/work-einvoice.ts`, `src/server/peppol-lookup.ts`, `src/server/access-point.ts`, `src/server/einvoice-sending.ts`).** From 1 January 2027 a Norwegian business must send e-invoices to buyers registered as receivers (ELMA), and the buyer's organisation number must be on sales documents from 1 January 2028 (bokføringsforskriften as amended 29 September 2026, Skatteetaten). A buyer is a participant by its country's scheme and organisation number (0192 Norway with its check digit, 0007 Sweden, 0184 Denmark), and the network is asked whether it receives each document type: the SML's NAPTR record at `base32(sha256(lowercase value))` (Peppol Policy for use of Identifiers 4.4.0 POLICY 7, the CNAME-to-NAPTR migration's own test vector holds it; NAPTR is the only record since February 2026), then the SMP (`commerce.peppol_receivers`, a day). Each decision is kept by address (`commerce.lead_decisions`, one row a person and store, the latest), deleted with the person by an erasure, never copied, under the `sales` purpose; written by `customers:write` while Deals is on, audited as `lead.*` with ids only.
